title: Long and short
hookLine: steps one and two: a long breath known as long, a short breath as short

lines: IN FOR FOUR, HOLD FOR SEVEN.
cards: Most breathing advice tells you to do something. Breathe in for four, hold for seven. Belly breathing.
Box breathing. Deep breaths before the presentation. Those have their uses.
But the first step of the Buddhist breathing discourse is stranger, and harder. It doesn't ask you to change anything: not the length, not the rhythm, not the depth. It asks you to notice.
And anyone who has tried it for sixty seconds knows how hard that is.

teach.h: BREATHING IN LONG, KNOW IT'S LONG.
teach.b: Here are steps one and two, from the Middle Length Discourses. Breathing in long, a person knows: I breathe in long. Breathing out long, they know: I breathe out long.
Breathing in short, they know it's short; breathing out short, the same. No instruction to make the breath long. The breath is whatever it is; your job is to know it.
The discourse on the foundations of mindfulness has a lovely picture for this: a skilled wood turner at his lathe, pulling the cord.
Making a long pull, he knows it's long. Making a short pull, he knows it's short. No fuss.
The knowing sits right alongside the doing. Why start here? Because the moment you watch the breath, you'll notice something funny: you start controlling it.
The breath gets stiff and self-conscious, like someone who knows they're being photographed.
Step one is learning to watch without grabbing: let the breath breathe itself, and let the knowing come along for the ride.

teach.h: NOT GOOD OR BAD: LONG OR SHORT.
teach.b: Long and short are useful words because they're simple.
Not good or bad, not deep enough, not right. Relaxed breathing tends to be longer; tense breathing, shorter.
So you start to notice which one you're in, which tells you how you actually are, before your mind has come up with a story about it.
That knowing, without judging and without fixing, is the root of everything that follows.

how: Buddhist breath meditation usually begins with simply knowing the breath as long or short, as the discourse describes, without controlling it.

o: knowing the breath as it is, unchanged
making each breath long and slow
switching between deep and quick breaths

games.q: what's inside the steps — tap the pairs.
p: a long breath, known as long
a short breath, known as short
knows a long pull from a short one

s: step one tells you to make the breath long and deep
it asks you to know the breath as it is, long or short.
the wood turner simile comes from the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness
he knows a long pull as long and a short pull as short.
trying to watch the breath often changes it at first
that's why step one is learning to watch without grabbing.

games.q: you're watching your breath, and it's short and tight. what does step two say to do?
games.why: breathing in short, you know: I breathe in short. no fixing, just knowing.

practice: For two minutes or five, let the breath do whatever it does, and on each in-breath and each out-breath, silently notice: long, or short.
If you catch yourself controlling it, that's fine: let go, and wait for the next breath to arrive on its own. If you can't tell long from short, just know: breathing in, breathing out.

wordCard.voice: Long and short. Steps one and two of the breathing discourse: knowing the breath as it is, without changing it.

orig.note: Pali: long; its partner in the steps is rassa, short.

carryVoice: Your line: just know it. Long or short, the breath is already telling you something. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: MN 118, Anapanasati Sutta: steps one and two
